Wagener originated in New York State in 1791 and became a widely respected 19th-century American apple, valued for its crisp, juicy, well-balanced tart-sweet flesh and, notably, its long storage life, holding good eating quality well into winter under proper cold storage conditions long before mechanical refrigeration was common. The medium, red-striped fruit is a genuine dual-purpose apple, good for fresh eating as well as cooking, and it holds a place in apple breeding history as a parent of the modern cold-hardy Idared. The precocious, productive tree bears young and reliably; harvest in fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for the longest keeping quality.

common_name: Swaar Apple (Dense Spicy-Sweet Hudson Valley Dutch Heirloom)

Swaar traces to the Dutch settlers of New York's Hudson Valley in the colonial era, taking its name from the Dutch word for 'heavy,' a direct reference to the unusually dense, weighty flesh of the fruit for its size. The large, dull yellow-green apple has rich, aromatic, spicy-sweet flesh considered by heirloom apple enthusiasts to be among the finest-flavored of the old Dutch-American varieties, and it stores exceptionally well, holding quality for months in proper cold storage. The tree is moderately vigorous and hardy, reflecting its long history of cultivation in the cold winters of the Hudson Valley; harvest in mid to late fall once fruit fully colors, and store cool for the best keeping.

Rhode Island Greening dates to around 1650, one of the oldest apple varieties native to New England, and it became one of the most celebrated American cooking apples of the 18th and 19th centuries, prized for large, green to yellow-green fruit with firm, tart, aromatic flesh widely considered among the very best for pie-making, since it holds its shape and delivers bright, well-balanced flavor when baked. The vigorous, spreading tree bears heavily once established, and the fruit keeps reasonably well in cool storage through much of the winter. While less commonly planted commercially today than in its heyday, Rhode Island Greening remains a favorite among heirloom orchardists and bakers who specifically seek out its superior pie-apple qualities.

Belle de Boskoop was discovered in the Dutch town of Boskoop in 1856 and became one of the most important cooking and baking apples in continental Europe, prized for large, rough-skinned, red-and-russet fruit with dense, notably tart, aromatic flesh that holds its shape beautifully under heat, making it outstanding for pies, tarte tatin, and applesauce. The tree is vigorous and long-lived, and the fruit stores exceptionally well, often keeping well into winter and even improving somewhat in flavor with a few weeks of storage. Its sharp, assertive tartness sets it apart from milder modern eating apples, making it a favorite specifically among European-style baking enthusiasts.

Court Pendu Gris is one of the oldest apple varieties still in cultivation, with a history some trace back to Roman times and documented in France and England for centuries, prized above all for blooming remarkably late in spring, well after most other apple varieties, which gives it outstanding natural resistance to the late frosts that damage or destroy the crop of earlier-flowering trees. The small, flattened, gray-russeted fruit has firm, dense, sharply flavored flesh that mellows and sweetens with storage, and the variety is an exceptional keeper, often holding good quality into late winter or even spring. Its low, spreading, naturally compact growth habit and remarkable frost avoidance have kept it valued by heirloom orchardists for centuries despite its modest fruit size.
